02Where this started

Deep-RF built the framework. Data rights turned a report into a feed.

The architecture came first, and it came from somewhere else.

Deep-RF proved the pattern — build the teleport, process at the edge, push RF observations into the UDL from several transponders, and let anyone downstream rebuild the picture. That framework is the reason this program did not have to invent its pipeline.

01
Teleport floor
Raw RF lands at the antenna. Enormous, continuous, and worthless to move.
02
Edge processing
Software sits as close to the antenna as possible and reduces the raw capture to a measured observation.
03
Low-latency text
What leaves the site is a small text payload — a PSD plot expressed as data, not an image. Low transport burden, low latency.
04
UDL
Published in schema. One publication, no per-consumer handling.
05
Any COP rebuilds it
The plot is reconstructed by whoever pulls it — our watch floor, or a high-side consumer, from the same record.

What the framework could not fix was ownership. SIOD had already paid for Kratos collection, but not for the rights to it. What arrived was a PDF. A person read the report and told someone else. Nothing was machine-readable at delivery, nothing could be correlated against a second source, and nothing reached a high-side consumer without a phone call.

Buying the data rights is what turned that report into a feed, and it is upstream of everything else on this page.

The expensive part of the work stays at the teleport. What crosses the network is small enough to move at machine speed and structured enough that nobody downstream needs to know which vendor produced it. That is why the program can add providers without adding integration debt.

Observed spectrum — carriers resolved above the noise floor.
03Orientation

If you come from SDA, read this first.

The physics is different. The problem shape is not.

Transponder
≈
An object you hold custody of
A single transponder carries many independent signals, and each signal is its own network — an RPA link, a C2 node, a commercial user. Because we monitor the whole transponder, we observe and report everything on it. Nobody outside can tell which signal we actually care about.
Noise floor
≈
Limiting magnitude
The sensitivity boundary of the instrument. Everything we detect sits above it — the question is by how little, and whether a fixed threshold would have caught it.
RF pattern of life
≈
Pattern of life / maneuver history
A baseline of recurrent normal behavior. Detection is deviation from the baseline, not a fixed threshold crossing. Same method as maneuver history, different observable.
Matched-modulation interference
≈
A low-signature object
Interference deliberately shaped to look like the traffic it is hiding in — same modulation, same shape, sitting just far enough above the legitimate carrier to get through. It presents almost no signature to key on, which is exactly what makes it hard to separate from the user's own signal.
TDOA / FDOA
≈
Two independent observation types
Time-difference produces lines of position that run near-parallel, so their own crossing is long and uncertain. Frequency-difference cuts across them at an angle and collapses the ambiguity. One technique alone leaves a solution you cannot tighten.
Geolocation error ellipse
≈
Covariance ellipsoid
An accuracy envelope around an estimate, not a measured error. Confidence rings nest around the same fix. It is only as honest as the model behind it — the SDA community calls that uncertainty realism.
Reference emitter
≈
Calibration source
A stable transmitter whose location we already know — a broadcast station, for instance. Geolocate it, measure how far the solution lands from truth, then apply that same correction to the interference. Without one, the bias stays in the answer.
UDL publish latency
≈
Observation-to-catalog timeline
The gap between observation and the moment anyone else can act on it. Twelve seconds at the median, from the teleport to a record any consumer can pull.

Why whole-transponder monitoring matters operationally

Because we observe and report on the entire transponder rather than a named signal, our collection posture reveals nothing about our interest. Every carrier on the passband gets the same treatment. An observer watching what we task cannot infer which network, which node, or which user we are actually concerned about.

Sourced definitions for each right-hand column are held separately and available on request.

04The stack

Five collectors, five different reasons.

Kratos is the data floor. Thirty transponders monitored today against a ceiling of thirty-two, across ten satellites.

Safran monitors three transponders on Eutelsat 36B, retasked in July from E21B, and includes geolocation in the base package.

Madfox is in UDL onboarding — four feeds paid and four delivering, across two satellites, with geolocation sensors scaling next.

Rebel Space is delivering from three ground sites and expanding aggressively to new teleports.

ViaSat / Darksaber brings on-orbit Ka in early August, DIU-funded.

Who pays for what, and at which rights tier

Every feed here is leased directly, with one exception. For Kratos, SIOD paid for the data but not the data rights. We bought the rights, and holding them is what made the data operationally relevant during Epic Fury.

We deliberately took R2, not R3. R3 would let us release publicly. We have no interest in that: this is DoD-leased bandwidth and the customer we report to is US Government. R2 permits sharing with US Government and JCO partners, which is the appropriate level for what this data actually is.

R3 may be needed later to support JCO allied partners once budget allows them, decided case by case against what each partner intends to do with derivative products.

Separately, the monitored ceiling now stands at thirty-two. We are at thirty and deliberately researching the final two. Meaningful transponders, not filler.

Eutelsat 36B is watched by three providers, not one

Safran and Madfox both observe 36B alongside Kratos. That is deliberate. It carries a heavy volume of EMI, it serves an important user, and the activity there is being missed by other reporting entities.

It is the clearest case on the portfolio for why overlapping coverage is worth paying for — three independent looks at the one place where something is actually happening.

Safran, Madfox and Rebel Space observe additional transponders and teleport-side spectrum not represented in the table above. Ka arrives in early August with ViaSat / Darksaber — commercial Ka monitoring we have never had.

06The stack

The standardized data schema is the foundational backbone of the capability.

Every provider publishes into the same UDL schema. That is what makes this a shared asset instead of five subscriptions.

2m

99%

0
BurstinessBurstinessHow evenly records arrive. Zero means a steady drip at the expected cadence. A high figure means long silences followed by bulk dumps — the same daily total, but useless for anything time-sensitive.

One schema means one integration. A consumer that can read a record from any provider can read a record from all of them, and a new provider joins the picture without anyone downstream changing anything. Maven, Wildhunt and EM&C pull the same records as the unclassified watch floor, with no hand-off, no conversion and no conversation.

The analogue is exact. This is the difference between a sensor operator emailing you a solution and a sensor publishing to the catalog. It is also why adding a provider costs us integration effort once rather than every time.

07The stack

Fusion is people, assisted.

Operators correlate across providers and build the product. BoxMica supports that work.

The layer above the data providers takes what is already in the UDL — from every source, not one — and produces bespoke insight rather than another feed. Corrected interference and spoofing data, RF change detection, pattern-of-life summaries, delivered machine-to-machine in H3 GEO schema.

This is early. It is real, and it is the layer where a second data source stops being redundancy and starts being evidence.

08The stack

One screen. Twenty-four feeds.

RAVEn Eye is where all of it becomes something a watch officer can act on.

Real-time spectrum and waterfall, per-transponder pattern-of-life baselinesPattern of lifeOccupied bandwidth, power, frequency and occupancy modelled per transponder over time. Alerts fire on standard deviations from baseline, not on fixed thresholds., event replay, and beam footprint overlay for spatial context. Alerts attach to the transponder that produced them.

The ticker at the bottom is the point: occupied bandwidth running two to three standard deviations from baseline. Nothing crossed a red line. The baseline moved.

Read the Safran figures against the retask

Safran was retasked in July from Eutelsat 21B to Eutelsat 36B. Records stopping on the E21B transponders after that date reflect our tasking decision, not a delivery failure, and are not counted against them. The uptime, burstiness and outage figures above are drawn from the tasked transponders.

This section is not an argument for cutting a vendor. It is the argument for having more than one, and for being able to prove real data metrics rather than accept a delivery claim.

10The stack

Geolocation — four sources, one funded healthily.

Geolocation is bought and delivered four different ways across this portfolio. They are not interchangeable and none of them is the primary capability.

SourceHow it is boughtStatus
SafranIncluded in the base package at no marginal costDelivering
KratosPurchased as a bank of five, on demand3 used, 2 remaining
SIODResults shared automatically under our data-rights agreement whenever SIOD runs one on a transponder we hold rights toNo cost to us
MadfoxSensor build-outEUCOM September
Rebel SpacePlatform roadmapIn development

The Safran arrangement is the one worth understanding. Their per-transponder rate is high — several multiples of a Kratos transponder including data and rights — but geolocations come with the package rather than being priced per event, and Kratos geolocations are bought individually and are not cheap. Twelve usable Safran geolocations since March is enough volume to close that gap entirely.

The arithmetic is held separately. The short version is that on current delivery they are cost-justified, and that verdict rests on geolocation volume rather than on the transponder line.

What geolocation is for depends entirely on who is asking

Today — DoD-leased bandwidth on the Kratos transponders. The end user wants geolocation above everything else. Attribution is the product they care about; detecting the EMI is what comes along with it. For this customer, geolocation is not a supporting layer, it is the point.

Looking to FY27 and JCO allied partners. The calculus inverts. What a partner nation needs is notification that interference exists and a clear read on whether to troubleshoot or move off the transponder — and help doing it. Identification and characterization carry that decision. Knowing where the signal originates matters far less to them than knowing what it is doing to their link.

Both are real requirements. They are not the same requirement, and a portfolio built for one will not serve the other well.

12Case — Eutelsat 36B

One transponder, one week, the whole chain.

Monitor, detect, characterise, and geolocate.

Eutelsat 36B, 20–24 July 2026. Interference ran on BEE5 and B2 across five consecutive days. What follows is the actual reporting, not a reconstruction.

Identification — the persistent signal

On BEE5, low-power CW interference distributed across the entire transponder with three peaks. Power varying over time. Observed throughout the day, every day of the reporting period.

Characterisation — a second signal on top of the first

On 21 July, a further CW interference appeared superimposed on the already-observed low-power CW, from 00:28 to 01:28 UTC.

That distinction is the capability. Calling a signal "superimposed on the one already there" is only possible if the first one was already modelled and understood. A monitor seeing this cold reports one anomaly. A monitor holding a baseline reports two separate things happening to the same transponder.

The week on B2

21 JulyB200:58–01:07  ·  05:47–09:07
21 JulyBEE523:38–23:58
22 JulyB200:07–00:27  ·  07:57–08:17
23 JulyB221:37–23:59
24 JulyB200:00–00:27

Geolocating the interference — and its limits

The 05:47–09:07 event on 21 July was worked for geolocation. The result is TDOA isolines only, using Eutelsat 21B as the mirror, with no reference emitter available for a TDOA/FDOA solution.

Safran's own caveat is the honest part: FDOA is the preferred method for CW signals, and it could not be used here. This is a bounded region, not a fix.

Then the question nobody usually asks — who is on this transponder?

Over the same period, Safran ran TDOA/TDOA geolocation using a two-mirror-satellite configuration against the legitimate carriers on B2. Three carriers were tested.

Carrier Eutelsat36D-B2-10998.902 MHz resolved to a mobile target moving at roughly 330 km/h, landing at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base. The other two carriers were also emitted from mobile targets.

Why this changes the priority

Interference on a transponder is a service problem. Interference on a transponder carrying mobile airborne users is a different problem, and until this was run, nothing in the reporting distinguished the two.

This is also what the extra tasking bought. Geolocating the victim rather than the interferer is not routine work, and it is the single piece of analysis that establishes why this transponder is important — and the lack of reports elsewhere is glaring.

13Case — C-band

Eight minutes, every eight minutes, for five weeks.

Interference nobody was looking for, on commercially leased bandwidth, traced to a regulatory compliance question.

The Rebel Space antenna site at Brewster, Washington detected C-band interference occurring persistently every eight minutes, causing user impacts on commercially leased bandwidth. Consistently between 3984.490 and 3984.814 MHz, across the whole collection period from 1 March to 7 April 2026.

Correlation

The observations correlate most strongly with Starlink Minisat V2 overpasses of the antenna — the Direct-to-Cell enabled variant.

The finding that makes it a case rather than a coincidence

1992 MHz × 2 = 3984 MHz

Starlink Direct-to-Cell ITU and FCC filings cover 1910–1915 MHz and 1990–1995 MHz. The interference sits consistently on the first harmonic of 1992 MHz, which is 3984 MHz — the band where it is being observed.

Those same filings, under FCC DA 24-1193, stipulate strict compliance with broadcast power limitations specifically to mitigate the risk of interference to adjacent spectrum users.

Pattern of life

The eight-minute cadence holds across the observation period. Tabular data confirms the same 3984 MHz signal at the same interval.

What this case actually demonstrates

Not every interference problem is hostile. This one appears to be an unintentional emission with a regulatory dimension, and it was still degrading a leased commercial link that a user depends on.

Finding it needed three things at once: persistent monitoring at a site that happened to be looking, a pattern-of-life baseline strong enough to establish an eight-minute cadence over five weeks, and publicly available information correlated against it to produce the harmonic explanation. No single provider on this page delivers all three alone.

Rebel Space's footprints are not yet where our AOR is. This is what they are already producing from the ones they have.

14What is being built

Safran — steady state first, then POI and EVO.

Today Safran delivers RF observations only. No points of interest, no event evolution records. Delivery is intermittent and the performance data shows it.

The stated trajectory is stable RF obs as priority one, then POI and EVO delivery into the UDL. Scope grows with funding and a corrected cost structure — and the cost structure is the live question.

What the machine metrics do not capture

Safran sends daily PDF reports that are thorough, substantive and genuinely useful. They do not show up anywhere in a uptime or burstiness figure, and they are a real part of what we are getting.

They have also proven willing to take on the more interesting taskings. The current event Simon raised is the example — Safran geolocated the actual user to demonstrate that the signal in question is an important one. That is analyst responsiveness, not feed volume, and it is not something every provider on this page would have done.

Why they were retained this cycle

The Kratos geolocation capability exists but is not funded as a standing line. Depending on a single geolocation source is not an acceptable posture, and the two providers do not cover the same areas. Safran stayed because a thin second source beats no second source — not because performance justified it.

Madfox — teleport partnerships that carry geolocation.

Madfox proposed eight feeds and could not fulfil eight. Four are paid and four are delivering across two satellites. UDL onboarding is underway.

What comes next is not more feeds. It is teleport relationships that put geolocation-capable sensors in two combatant command areas.

What the spend is actually buying

Part of what the current spend buys is the coverage expansion and the UDL integration themselves. Those are large lifts for the money. What is being bought is not this month's data — it is a sensor in the right place with a schema-compliant pipe attached.

16What is being built

Three sites delivering today. Every satellite they can see sits between 180°E and 53°W — the Western hemisphere. Our problem is over Africa, the Middle East and Eastern Europe.

This is not a performance failure. It is geometry, and geometry has a schedule.

What we would do with scaling funds

With FY27 dollars, the lever is partner-nation tasking across EUCOM and PACOM. Once we know where the user need actually sits, we can help Rebel prioritise which teleport partnerships to sign first — which turns their expansion roadmap into our coverage plan rather than a coincidence.

17What is being built

ViaSat / Darksaber — on-orbit Ka, early August.

Commercial Ka monitoring we have never had, from orbit, funded by DIU.

The data-rights dispute is resolved on amended terms. A working MVP integration has been demonstrated. Delivery begins in early August at no cost to this budget for roughly eight months.

The integration story is done. The scaling story is not: the cost structure beyond the DIU window is unknown. No program dollars should be committed against it until that is pinned.

18What is being built

PACOM and allied partner expansion.

This was the original priority. It remains the direction of travel, contingent on a healthy FY27.

If a specific requirement lands, there are two paths and they are not the same path.

Procurement. Kratos can add relevant Pacific coverage immediately against the same architecture and schema — this is capacity, not integration. It is available now, with dollars, at a likely higher unit cost.

Development. Rebel Space and Madfox expand into the footprint, and Safran too as they build partnerships that bring their cost down and reach areas Kratos does not cover. Slower, cheaper, and it produces a supplier base rather than a bill.

Stated plainly

We can buy Pacific-relevant data immediately if the money appears. What we are doing instead — deliberately — is developing smaller providers who are more agile, more affordable and more responsive. That work only continues if the program survives intact.

19Single provider

If August arrives with no plus-up.

At current budget dollars the program cuts to Kratos and Alethia. Nothing else survives.

  • The second source. Cross-provider corroboration ends. A quiet transponder and an absent provider become indistinguishable again.
  • Most geolocation. Safran's included geolocations end. Madfox's September EUCOM delivery does not happen. Rebel's in-development capability does not arrive. Kratos retains two remaining from the purchased bank, and more only with new money.
  • Rebel's Q3 and Q4 sites. Usingen and the Canary Islands are partly funded here. The AOR footprint does not appear on schedule.
  • Madfox UDL onboarding. Stops mid-integration, sunk work unrecovered, and the Belgium and Colombia teleport relationships go with it.
  • The fusion layer. Multi-source correlation with one source is not correlation.
  • Cross-provider grading. Provider health monitoring survives, but with one supplier there is nothing left to compare against.

The part that does not show up on a capability chart

Cutting to one provider does not just narrow the picture. It ends our ability to develop competitors and leaves us with a single known monopoly supplier — who will price and prioritise accordingly, for as long as that position holds.

The small providers on this page are being nurtured on purpose. A competitive pool is what produces better products, better prices and faster responsiveness. Rebuilding one after it has been dismantled costs far more than sustaining it.

Most of what is lost here is not capability we are running today. It is capability we are three to five months from running, with the integration cost already paid.

20Single provider

What survives is still real.

This is not an argument that the mission ends. It is an argument about what kind of mission is left.

  • Kratos. Thirty transponders against a ceiling of thirty-two, ten satellites, 99% live-cadence uptime, twelve-second median publish lag, full data rights into the UDL and out to the high side.
  • Alethia RAVEn Eye. The operating picture, and the only way anyone sees the Kratos data at all. Provider health comes with it, at the current level of fidelity rather than the expanded one.
  • Ka, for eight months. The ViaSat / Darksaber window is DIU-funded and does not fall with the budget. What is deferred is what happens after it.

That is a credible single-source RF observation capability over CENTCOM and EUCOM, delivering to the UDL at machine speed. Four months ago it was a PDF. It is a real gain and should not be described as anything less.

Detection survives. Corroboration does not. Every forward capability on this page — the September geolocation, the Q4 sensor in the right hemisphere, the Pacific option, the supplier base itself — stops rather than arrives.

The integration we have already paid for does not vanish on day one. It stalls. And a long enough gap without funds is how it goes for good: these are small companies with other customers, and a provider left waiting will point its roadmap at whoever is still buying.

21On the horizon

POI to Emitter Location — the schema everyone is standing on.

The whole community publishes interference geolocation into a UDL schema that was never designed for it.

Point of Interest was built for a different purpose. It became the interference schema because it was the closest thing already in the UDL and it worked — which is a perfectly reasonable way for a standard to happen, and a bad place to stay.

Emitter Location is purpose-built for this. It is the better schema, it exists, and it is the right destination.

Today
POI
EM&C is the program of record. Maven, Wildhunt and our own RAVEn Eye all flight-follow the program of record onto POI.
Bridge
Dual publication
With funds, a small integration increment with each provider so they push to both Emitter Location and POI. Failover becomes trivial and nothing breaks mid-transition.
Destination
Emitter Location
The program of record moves, the community follows, and Emitter Location becomes the default.

For us, the upgrade is a minimal task. That is not the constraint.

The long pole

The program of record has to move, and that is the slow part. They have already expressed the desire to do it — the limit is that they work at the speed of contracts.

Which makes the sequencing the real work. The whole stakeholder community has to be on board before Emitter Location becomes the default, not after. Move the default first and you strand every consumer still reading POI.

The near-term ask is modest and it buys optionality: fund dual publication with each provider now, so that when the program of record is ready, the transition is a switch rather than a project.
